messages.author: 5a8bfcb87fd22c3b
messages.subject: Identifiability in multinomial logistic models
parts:
Hello,

I've been working on a categorical logit model in Stan that's trying to measure the relative ability of subjects. I have a total of ~500 subjects, but in each data point only 10 subjects are present and one is selected. So in each data point, there is a random subset of 10 of the ~500 subjects. The key part of the model looks like this:


for (i in 1:n) {
 vector[10] x;
 
 for (j in 1:10) {
    x[j] <- subject_effects[subjects[i][j]];
 }

 res[i] ~ categorical_logit(x);
}

Because softmax is invariant under the addition of a constant, one solution the Stan manual offers is to fix a category to 0 to act as a reference category. However, in my model, I can set one of the subjects to 0 as a reference but that reference won't be present except for whichever data points include that particular subject.


My question is: does that matter for identifiability or does it still identify the model to set one of the subjects as a reference? If it's inappropriate, is the only solution to set strong priors on the subject effects? Since I really only care about the relative differences between subjects, does it matter either way?

Thanks,
Rick

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Identifiability in multinomial logistic models
parts:
> On Feb 28, 2016, at 12:24 AM, ricka...@gmail.com wrote:
>
> Hello,
>
> I've been working on a categorical logit model in Stan that's trying to measure the relative ability of subjects. I have a total of ~500 subjects, but in each data point only 10 subjects are present and one is selected. So in each data point, there is a random subset of 10 of the ~500 subjects. The key part of the model looks like this:
>
>
> for (i in 1:n) {
> vector[10] x;
>
> for (j in 1:10) {
> x[j] <- subject_effects[subjects[i][j]];
> }
>
> res[i] ~ categorical_logit(x);
> }
>
With the new vectorization, you should be able to write this as

res[i] ~ categorical_logit(subject_effects[subjects[i]]);

Assuming that you declared subject_effects as a vector.

> Because softmax is invariant under the addition of a constant, one solution the Stan manual offers is to fix a category to 0 to act as a reference category. However, in my model, I can set one of the subjects to 0 as a reference but that reference won't be present except for whichever data points include that particular subject.
>
>
> My question is: does that matter for identifiability or does it still identify the model to set one of the subjects as a reference?

If all the subjects interact, then it's technically enough.
But if there's a partition of the subjects across which they
don't interact, then no.
> If it's inappropriate, is the only solution to set strong priors on the subject effects?

You can do that. You should have priors based on what you
know about the problem in any case. In any case, a hierarchical
prior on subject_effects would be in order.
> Since I really only care about the relative differences between subjects, does it matter either way?

What you can't have in Stan is an unidentified model. Putting
a prior on the subject_effects will identify it, but it's only
a soft kind of identification in the total log density. It's usually
better to have the likelihood itself be identified as well.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Identifiability in multinomial logistic models
parts:
Thanks for the tips - especially about vectorizing the categorical_logit statement.

Unfortunately, the subjects don't all interact and there's no natural reference category, so my solution was improper.

I should have mentioned that I do have a hierarchical prior on subject_effects with a half-cauchy on the variance and a zero-mean. Ideally I would reframe the problem to include a reference category but it just doesn't seem possible here.

With the priors, here is the summary of lp:
lp__                       -40896.22    3.67 46.21 -40983.73 -40928.47 -40896.32 -40864.14 -40807.07   159 1.01

And the statistics:
accept_stat__    stepsize__       treedepth__  n_leapfrog__  n_divergent__  
 Min.   :0.00   Min.   : 0.0026   Min.   : 1   Min.   :   1   Min.   :0.000  
 1st Qu.:0.81   1st Qu.: 0.0256   1st Qu.: 7   1st Qu.: 127   1st Qu.:0.000  
 Median :0.93   Median : 0.0339   Median : 7   Median : 127   Median :0.000  
 Mean   :0.84   Mean   : 0.0649   Mean   : 7   Mean   : 161   Mean   :0.044  
 3rd Qu.:0.98   3rd Qu.: 0.0445   3rd Qu.: 7   3rd Qu.: 127   3rd Qu.:0.000  
 Max.   :1.00   Max.   :14.3855   Max.   :10   Max.   :1023   Max.   :1.000

Would you consider this a soft identification on the log density? I'm not sure how to interpret these to diagnose identifiability.

The only other solution that comes to mind for me is to fit multiple binary logit models with 10 data points per trial and the selected subject labeled as 1 and the others as 0. Any thoughts on this approach compared to what I'm doing now?

Thanks,
Rick

If they don't all interact, then they won't be calibrated
to each other anyway!

If the lp__ is mixing that well, you should be fine given
that the other quantities of interest are mixing.

messages.author: a8b6459b77c849fe
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Identifiability in multinomial logistic models
parts:
There are two possible interpretations of "the subjects don't all interact":

1. There are subjects s1 and s2 that never appear together in a case i.

2. Creating a graph where the subjects are nodes, with an edge between s1 and s2 whenever s1 and s2 appear together in a case, this graph is not fully connected: there is at least one pair of subjects with no path connecting them.

#1 isn't a problem by itself, but #2 could be a problem.

Strictly speaking, even with a fully connected graph you have likelihood non-identifiability, but the large number of subjects plus your prior on the effects should greatly reduce the posterior correlation. If the graph is not connected but each connected component has a large number of subjects in it, the situation is similar. The problem case would be if there exists one or more connected component with a small number of subjects in it; that would be a small group of subjects that never get compared, even indirectly, to a larger group of subjects.

I have some blog posts that don't directly address your problem, but which you might find useful in thinking about these kinds of issues. See

    http://bayesium.com/full-dummy-coding-for-nominal-variables/ 

and maybe

    http://bayesium.com/a-symmetric-effects-prior/

and

    http://bayesium.com/implementing-the-symmetric-effects-prior/

(Think of "subject" as a nominal input variable with 500 levels.)
